analysis.one_liner: Phases lead out of paint, plumbing, food packaging, gasoline, and batteries, and funds lead-poisoning prevention and abatement.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved the bill with amendments, but it sat on the Senate calendar for 15 months and never received a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned or limited lead in products people touch every day: paint, plumbing pipes and fixtures, solder, food cans and packaging, wine bottle foils, toys, and gasoline sold in large cities. It required battery retailers to take back used lead-acid batteries for recycling and banned dumping them in landfills. It also set up lab certification, worker training, public education, and research programs, and in the committee-approved version required sellers and landlords of older homes to disclose known lead-paint hazards to buyers and renters.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under seven, who the bill's findings describe as most vulnerable to lead's permanent neurological damage [S4]; families living in older housing with lead paint; construction and abatement workers; and the general public exposed to lead through drinking water, food packaging, and soil [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and residents of older housing

how_it_helps.text: Bans products with significant lead content, including paint above 0.06 percent lead, plumbing fittings and fixtures above 2 percent, toys, curtain weights, and pesticides above 0.1 percent [S4].
Directs EPA to ban the sale of lead solder used in plumbing, which leaches lead into drinking water [S4].
Prohibits food cans with solder above 0.2 percent lead and wine bottle foils above 0.1 percent lead, and treats food in over-limit containers as adulterated under food safety law [S4].
Bans the sale of leaded gasoline in metropolitan areas of 250,000 or more people and forbids selling leaded gas cheaper than unleaded at the same station [S4].
Bans putting lead-acid batteries in landfills or incinerators and requires retailers, wholesalers, and manufacturers to accept used batteries for recycling, with posted notices and labels [S4].

Sets up lab certification for lead testing in paint, dust, soil, and blood; training curricula for abatement workers and supervisors; public education campaigns; and grants to universities for Centers for the Prevention of Lead Poisoning [S4].
The committee-reported version added lead disclosure rules for home sales and leases of pre-1978 housing, mortgage disclosures, and state registries of properties with significant lead hazards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of lead-containing products — paint, plumbing fittings and solder, food cans and packaging, wine foils, ceramics, and batteries — would bear compliance, reformulation, record-keeping, and take-back costs, some of which could be passed to consumers in modestly higher prices. Taxpayers would fund the grant, research, and education programs, authorized at roughly $25 million in the first year declining to $22 million by fiscal 1994 [S4].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on a wide range of manufacturers — paint, plumbing, canning, packaging, glass and ceramics, and battery makers — and some costs would likely reach consumers through higher prices; the bill itself acknowledges hardship, authorizing delays for wine foil makers holding large noncomplying inventories [S4].

The bill requires extensive notification, inventory, and certification paperwork for manufacturers, processors, and importers of any product above 0.1 percent lead, a real administrative burden for smaller firms [S4].

It preempts state and local battery recycling rules that lack the federal labeling, notice, and collection requirements, limiting states' ability to go further, though states may still impose deposits [S4].

It contains carve-outs that weaken the headline bans: exemptions for artists' paint, medical, defense, nuclear, and mining products, a waiver for collectible toys and scale models, and a temporary exemption for industrial paint, allowing continued lead in those channels [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong: the bill's own findings call lead poisoning the most prevalent environmentally caused disease among American children, with permanent neurological effects [S4]. The compliance costs fall on a broad set of manufacturers but are spread thin per product, and the bill includes phase-ins, performance standards, and hardship delays to soften them. The main honest criticisms are the paperwork burden, the exemptions, and the modest federal preemption of state battery rules — serious design questions, but small next to the stakes of childhood lead exposure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its subcommittee and the full Environment and Public Works Committee with amendments, was placed on the Senate's legislative calendar in October 1991, and then sat there without ever being brought up for a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 7, 1991 by Senator Harry Reid with fourteen original cosponsors, and read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee [S6].
The Subcommittee on Toxic Substances approved it with amendments favorably on April 17, 1991 [S6].
The full committee ordered it reported favorably with amendments on August 1, 1991, and reported it to the Senate on October 8, 1991, with written report 102-179 [S6].
The reported version expanded the bill, adding lead disclosure requirements for residential sales, leases, and mortgages, a wine lead tolerance, and ceramic ware and crystal leaching standards [S3].
It was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 263 on October 8, 1991 [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred; the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993 with the bill still on the calendar [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of lead-containing products — paint, plumbing, packaging, canning, and battery makers — avoided the compliance and reformulation costs the bill would have imposed. Children and residents of older housing got no federal lead protections from this bill, though lead-disclosure rules for housing later passed separately.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew bipartisan support — 16 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors, with Republican Sen. Jim Jeffords an original cosponsor — and cleared its Senate committee without a recorded dissent, but never reached a floor vote where the partisan split would have been tested [S5][S6].

industries.industry: Lead-acid battery makers, retailers, and recyclers
industries.note: The bill bans landfilling batteries and makes retailers, wholesalers, and manufacturers the permanent legal channel for collecting and recycling used batteries, with mandatory take-back and labeling. It imposes compliance costs but locks in their role as the recycling system, and battery makers gain a steady stream of returned batteries as feedstock [S4].

Paint above 0.06 percent lead could no longer be made or sold, with only a temporary exemption for industrial paint and a carve-out for artists' paint. Abatement standards and training programs would also create a new lead-paint remediation market [S4].
The bill directs EPA to ban lead plumbing solder and cap lead in fittings and fixtures at 2 percent, forcing reformulation of pipes and fixtures that leach lead into drinking water [S4].

Food cans with solder above 0.2 percent lead and packaging with intentionally added lead would be phased out, and food in over-limit containers would be deemed adulterated — compliance costs for canners and packaging suppliers that protect consumers from lead in food [S4].

Leaded gasoline could no longer be sold for on-road use in metro areas of 250,000 or more, or priced below unleaded at the same station, accelerating the phase-out of a major airborne lead source [S4].
Lead wine bottle foils above 0.1 percent would be banned, and ceramic ware and crystal would face leaching standards, with nonconforming items treated as adulterated goods [S3].

industries.industry: Environmental testing labs and abatement contractors
industries.note: Federal certification programs for lead testing labs, training curricula for abatement workers, standards for abatement products, and grants to states and universities create a certified market for lead inspection and removal services [S3].
